submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole fires on concrete, tangible, hands-on content: words naming physical objects, tools, materials, body parts and foods (hammer, screwdriver, copper wire, boulders, broth, hand) and the manual actions performed on them (splice, weave, hammer, slice, dig, tighten, solder), with the peak landing on the content word or on the function word beside it (e.g. 'or' in 'hatchet or ax', '-' in 'Doyle-Murray'). It stays near zero on abstract, cognitive, institutional or symbolic text (theory, policy, method, committee, budget, algorithm, source code), which is the other end of the same concrete-to-abstract axis.

On the second Tuesday of March, the city council convened in the renovated chambers on the fourth floor of the municipal building to review the proposed operating budget for the coming fiscal year. The chair opened the session by noting that revenue projections had been revised downward for the third consecutive quarter and that the finance department would therefore present three alternative spending scenarios rather than the single plan circulated the previous month. Each scenario, she explained, rested on a different assumption about the growth of the commercial tax base and the likely trajectory of state transfers, and none of them assumed any increase in the property tax rate beyond the cap approved by the voters in the autumn referendum.

The finance director then walked the council through the first scenario, which he described as the most conservative of the three. Under this projection, departmental allocations would remain flat in nominal terms, which in practice meant a reduction of roughly two percent once inflation was taken into account. He noted that the parks department and the library system would absorb most of the adjustment, since the debt service on the new water treatment facility was fixed by contract and could not be renegotiated before the next biennium. Several council members pressed him on the assumptions behind the wage growth forecast, and he conceded that the model had been calibrated on data from the metropolitan region rather than from the city itself, a limitation that the research staff had flagged in an appendix.

The second scenario, by contrast, assumed that the state would release the withheld transportation funds in the spring, allowing the city to shift a portion of its capital budget onto the operating ledger without increasing the overall deficit. The council's budget analyst cautioned that this assumption was speculative, because the allocation formula had been rewritten during the previous legislative session and the implementing regulations had not yet been published. A lengthy discussion followed about the difference between committed and uncommitted reserves and about whether the fund balance policy adopted two years earlier required a minimum of eight percent or twelve percent of general revenues. The city attorney was asked to prepare a memorandum on the question before the next reading of the ordinance.

Public comment began shortly after seven. A retired teacher argued that the proposed reductions to the library system would disproportionately affect residents in the eastern wards, where access to broadband remained unreliable and where the branch had become a de facto community center. A representative of the chamber of commerce urged the council to defer any decision until the results of the regional economic impact study were available, warning that uncertainty itself carried a cost for employers considering relocation. A graduate student presented a statistical analysis suggesting that the revenue forecasts were biased downward, and the chair thanked her for the submission while reminding the audience that public comment was not the appropriate venue for a technical debate about the model specification.
